paragraphs: Assigning a value to a training example requires deciding what its contribution should be measured against. Existing data Shapley methods answer this question within a fixed dataset. That makes the valuation tied to a particular collection and leaves no direct way to value a point outside it. This paper instead defines a point’s contribution relative to an underlying data distribution.

The resulting framework, distributional Shapley, brings statistical behavior into the definition of value. The authors prove properties including stability when either individual data points or the underlying distribution are perturbed. These results matter because a valuation should not depend excessively on small changes in the data used to establish it.

The authors use these properties to build an estimation algorithm with formal guarantees. They report that it runs two orders of magnitude faster than leading algorithms for conventional data Shapley, while computing the new distributional valuation. Applications across diverse datasets and a data market setting demonstrate the framework’s practical utility.
icml-2020-a-distributional-framework-for.tldr: Distributional Shapley values data relative to a population, enabling stable valuations and a fast estimation algorithm with formal guarantees.

paragraphs: Canonical polyadic decomposition represents a tensor through simpler components. Computing that representation can be expensive, so sketched algorithms reduce the work involved in alternating least squares updates. This paper studies such algorithms with proximal regularization and asks how much sketching should be used as the decomposition progresses.

The theoretical contribution establishes a sublinear convergence rate under two conditions satisfied by many popular sketching methods. The algorithmic contribution, CPD-MWU, selects the sketching rate adaptively at each iteration. This makes the amount of approximation part of the iterative procedure rather than a single fixed choice for the entire computation.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show different benefits for different tensors. For noisy tensors, CPD-MWU reaches comparable accuracy to standard CPD in less time, often about half. For ill-conditioned tensors, it achieves an order-of-magnitude lower relative error within the same time budget. On one representative real dataset, average residual errors are 20% below CPRAND-MIX and 44% below SPALS. These findings support adapting sketching to the evolving computation.
icml-2020-adaptive-sketching-for-fast-an.tldr: CPD-MWU adaptively chooses sketching rates to accelerate tensor decomposition, with conditional convergence guarantees and empirical accuracy gains.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive translation predicts an entire target sequence in parallel, enabling faster decoding. Its challenge is organizing those predictions into the correct word order without the sequential dependencies used by autoregressive models. Ordinary cross entropy adds another difficulty: a small shift in token positions can receive a large penalty even when much of the predicted content is appropriate.

Aligned cross entropy, or AXE, changes how the training loss compares predictions with the target. A differentiable dynamic program finds the best monotonic alignment between them and assigns loss using that alignment. Monotonicity preserves sequence order while allowing the comparison to accommodate positional shifts. The training signal therefore depends on an aligned correspondence rather than rigid position-by-position matching.

The authors apply AXE to conditional masked language models and report substantial improvements on major WMT benchmarks, reaching a new state of the art for non-autoregressive models. The finding shows that the way a loss measures sequence disagreement can materially affect translation quality, alongside the model’s parallel prediction design.
icml-2020-aligned-cross-entropy-for-non-.tldr: AXE trains parallel translation models using an alignment-aware loss, reducing sensitivity to token shifts and improving reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming aims to let users describe how data are generated while inference machinery handles the resulting calculations. In practice, the mathematical parameterization of a model can strongly affect inference performance. Users may therefore need to rewrite an otherwise suitable model in ways that are difficult to anticipate from the modeling problem itself.

This paper argues that those transformations should be automated. It demonstrates how mechanisms in recent modeling frameworks can implement non-centering and related reparameterizations. The contribution makes alternative expressions of a model available to inference algorithms without requiring users to perform each transformation manually.

The authors introduce two inference approaches built on this capability. One uses interleaved sampling; the other uses a variational formulation that searches continuously over parameterizations. Across a range of models, these approaches support robust inference and can produce samplers more efficient than the best fixed parameterization. The result suggests that selecting or combining parameterizations during inference can offer benefits beyond choosing one representation in advance.
icml-2020-automatic-reparameterisation-o.tldr: Automated model reparameterization enables inference methods that can outperform the best fixed parameterization across the studied models.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph from observations requires understanding which structures the data can distinguish. For acyclic graphs, equivalence is commonly described through conditional independence relationships. When feedback cycles are allowed, however, those relationships may miss distributional information that helps identify structure. The paper addresses this mismatch within linear Gaussian causal models.

The authors define two structures as distributionally equivalent when they can generate exactly the same collection of data distributions. This gives a unified definition covering graphs with and without cycles. They also introduce the weaker concept of quasi-equivalence and show that it describes the extent to which structure can be identified from observational data.

Analytic and graphical methods provide ways to characterize equivalence between structures. The paper additionally proposes a score-based learning method that handles both cyclic and acyclic graphs successfully. Together, these contributions connect a definition of indistinguishability with a practical structure-learning approach, while retaining the observational identifiability boundary expressed through quasi-equivalence.
icml-2020-characterizing-distribution-eq.tldr: The paper characterizes distributional equivalence and observational identifiability for linear Gaussian causal graphs, including graphs with feedback cycles.

paragraphs: Combining users’ collections into a shared set is a basic data operation, but publishing the result can expose information about individual contributions. This paper studies set union under the global model of differential privacy. Each user contributes a subset of items, and the possible item universe may be infinitely large.

The goal is to release as many distinct contributed items as possible while satisfying an epsilon-delta differential privacy requirement. The output must be a subset of the actual union, so usefulness is measured by how much of that union the algorithm can retain. This formulation makes the privacy constraint and the desired output explicit within the same optimization problem.

The authors design new algorithms and report significant improvements over the best previously known methods. Private text analysis illustrates the relevance: discovering words, sentences, or n-grams from users’ documents is a set-union task. Better algorithms can therefore support broader discovery from private collections while operating under the stated formal privacy requirement.
icml-2020-differentially-private-set-uni.tldr: New algorithms improve how many contributed items can be released in a set union subject to differential privacy.

paragraphs: One-class classification learns about a class of interest and uses that knowledge to recognize departures from it. Classical methods can require carefully designed features, particularly for images. Deep approaches reduce that burden but introduce other difficulties: transformation-based methods need suitable domain-specific transformations, while representation-based one-class losses can suffer from collapse.

DROCC is designed to apply across most standard domains without side information and to resist representation collapse. Its central assumption is geometric: examples from the target class lie on a well-sampled, locally linear manifold of low dimension. This assumption supplies structure for the learning problem without requiring a specially chosen set of transformations for each domain.

The authors evaluate DROCC in two one-class problem settings using tabular data, images, audio, and time series. They report strong effectiveness across these domains and accuracy improvements of up to 20% over the state of the art in anomaly detection. These are empirical gains under the studied settings, with the manifold assumption remaining central to the proposed approach.
icml-2020-drocc-deep-robust-one-class-cl.tldr: DROCC uses a low-dimensional manifold assumption for robust one-class learning and reports anomaly-detection gains across several data domains.

paragraphs: Fractal patterns have been observed in networks across diverse applications, motivating models that express this structure explicitly. This paper introduces Fractal Gaussian Networks, a family of sparse random geometric graphs with mathematically defined and analytically tractable fractal behavior. The aim is to make fractality something that can be modeled and investigated systematically.

A parameter controls the strength of the fractal structure. Varying it continuously connects familiar purely random geometric graphs with networks exhibiting increasingly fractal behavior. The underlying spatial geometry comes from Gaussian Multiplicative Chaos, which supplies the model’s source of fractality. This construction places different degrees of fractal organization within a single parameterized family.

The authors explore whether observed network data can reveal the presence of fractality and how the model’s parameters can be estimated. They also introduce a natural stochastic block model within the same setting to examine fractal community structure. These directions connect the graph construction to questions about detecting, measuring, and organizing fractality in observed networks.
icml-2020-fractal-gaussian-networks-a-sp.tldr: Fractal Gaussian Networks provide a tractable sparse graph family with adjustable fractality and extensions for studying community structure.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning and Q-learning remain popular because they are straightforward to use and often perform well, despite known divergence problems. Gradient TD alternatives offer stronger foundations but can be more complicated to tune. Instability in large neural learning systems makes this tradeoff more pressing than occasional failures might suggest.

The paper introduces TD with Regularized Corrections, or TDRC, to balance practical performance, ease of use, and soundness. The authors describe it as behaving as well as TD where TD works well while remaining sound in cases where TD diverges. Its purpose is to reduce the practical cost of choosing a more principled learning method.

The empirical investigation covers prediction and control, using both linear and nonlinear function approximation. The results suggest that Gradient TD methods could be preferable to conventional TD and Q-learning. That conclusion is deliberately qualified: the evidence supports their potential as practical alternatives across the studied problems, rather than establishing universal superiority for every reinforcement-learning task.
icml-2020-gradient-temporal-difference-l.tldr: TDRC seeks to combine TD’s practical performance with sound corrections, and experiments suggest Gradient TD methods could be competitive alternatives.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using observations collected under other behavior. In settings such as healthcare, an estimate needs scrutiny before it can inform deployment. Confidence intervals alone may be insufficient when data are noisy, limited, or confounded. This paper makes the observations driving an estimate easier for experts to inspect.

The method identifies transitions whose removal would substantially change the evaluation result. It then applies rules to select which influential observations should be presented to domain experts. This creates a possible human-AI review process: the algorithm directs attention toward consequential evidence, and experts assess whether that evidence supports the evaluation.

The authors derive exact influence functions for fitted Q-evaluation using kernel-based and linear least-squares function classes, as well as for importance-sampling methods. Experiments involving medical simulations and intensive care data show that the approach can expose limitations in evaluation and improve robustness. Its contribution is an interpretable route to checking estimates, rather than a guarantee that an evaluated policy is safe.
icml-2020-interpretable-off-policy-evalu.tldr: Highlighting transitions that strongly affect off-policy estimates helps experts identify weaknesses and improve evaluation robustness.

paragraphs: Unnormalized density models describe relative density without requiring an explicitly normalized probability expression. This paper develops a shared method for evaluating and training such models using only the gradient of the model’s unnormalized log-density. It uses a learned Stein discrepancy to measure disagreement between the observed data distribution and the model.

The discrepancy depends on a vector-valued function evaluated on the data. The authors represent this function with a neural network and optimize it to make the discrepancy large. This learned function provides a way to expose differences between data and model, yielding a goodness-of-fit test that outperforms existing methods on high-dimensional data.

Training reverses the objective for the density model: its parameters are adjusted to reduce the discrepancy. The authors report that this procedure can fit large unnormalized models faster than existing approaches. The same discrepancy thus supports both comparison and learning, giving a common framework for detecting a model’s mismatch and then optimizing the model to reduce it.
icml-2020-learning-the-stein-discrepancy.tldr: A neural-network estimate of Stein discrepancy supports both goodness-of-fit testing and faster training of large unnormalized density models.

paragraphs: Generating a promising molecular structure is only part of drug design: the molecule also needs a feasible synthesis route. This paper introduces Policy Gradient for Forward Synthesis, or PGFS, to incorporate synthetic accessibility directly into molecular generation. It frames design as a sequence of virtual chemical construction steps.

The agent begins with commercially available molecules and applies valid chemical reactions at each step. Its search therefore proceeds through a synthesis process rather than proposing structures without routes. The resulting reinforcement-learning environment is challenging because it combines an immense state space with high-dimensional continuous actions and a hierarchical action structure.

PGFS achieves reported state-of-the-art performance for generating structures with high QED and clogP. The authors also conduct an in-silico proof of concept involving three HIV targets. These findings support the proposed approach to computational molecular design; the target validation described is computational. More broadly, the work presents end-to-end learning over forward synthesis as a way to expand exploration of synthesizable chemical space.
icml-2020-learning-to-navigate-the-synth.tldr: PGFS learns to design molecules through valid virtual reaction sequences, integrating synthesis routes into reinforcement-learning-based molecular generation.

paragraphs: A single denoiser is often trained to handle a range of noise levels by sampling those levels uniformly. This paper questions whether equal allocation is the best use of training examples. The central problem is how to distribute samples across noise levels when the same estimator must serve the whole range.

The authors formulate this choice through minimax risk optimization, making performance under the most demanding conditions central to selecting the sampling distribution. They derive a dual ascent algorithm for finding the optimal distribution. Its convergence guarantee requires the admissible set of estimators to be closed and convex, so the mathematical structure of the estimator family matters.

Deep neural networks generally involve nonconvex admissible sets. In that case, the stated convergence result applies to a solution of the convex relaxation rather than directly establishing the original nonconvex optimum. The paper discusses practical implementation and evaluates the algorithm with linear estimators and deep networks, treating the training distribution itself as a quantity to optimize.
icml-2020-one-size-fits-all-can-we-train.tldr: The paper optimizes how denoising examples are allocated across noise levels, with convergence guarantees that depend on the estimator family.

paragraphs: Recommendation data often contain ordered categories, such as ratings or play counts grouped into levels. Converting these observations into binary indicators discards distinctions between the levels. OrdNMF is a probabilistic non-negative matrix factorization model designed to retain that ordering and use the more informative representation directly.

The model generalizes Bernoulli-Poisson factorization and Poisson factorization applied to binarized observations. Its latent-factor formulation provides a way to represent recommendation data while preserving their ordinal character. The authors also develop an efficient variational inference algorithm using a suitable augmentation of the model, connecting the computation to variational Poisson factorization.

A key practical result is that the algorithm retains the scalability of Poisson factorization and can handle very large sparse datasets. Recommendation experiments cover both explicit and implicit feedback, and OrdNMF outperforms the two stated approaches when they operate on binarized data. The findings support preserving ordered feedback while maintaining a computational approach suited to sparse recommendation settings.
icml-2020-ordinal-non-negative-matrix-fa.tldr: OrdNMF preserves ordered recommendation feedback and improves reported results over binarized factorization methods while retaining scalability.

paragraphs: An agent manipulating objects needs to connect an understanding of their geometry with decisions about what to do next. This paper calls that combined ability geometric planning. It introduces PackIt, a virtual environment built to evaluate that ability and potentially support learning it through interaction.

The task is to pack a collection of objects into a box with limited space by taking a sequence of actions. This links spatial understanding to planning: the agent must use information about the objects and available space as it decides how to proceed. The authors also use an evolutionary algorithm to construct challenging packing tasks, providing a way to generate demanding instances of the problem.

The paper studies several kinds of baselines, including model-free learning methods, heuristics, and search-based optimization. The search methods assume access to a model of the environment. These comparisons establish different approaches to the benchmark, while the environment itself supplies a focused setting for investigating the combination of geometry and sequential action.
icml-2020-packit-a-virtual-environment-f.tldr: PackIt benchmarks geometric planning through sequential object packing, with generated challenges and several classes of baseline methods.

paragraphs: PoWER-BERT speeds up BERT inference by removing redundant word vectors from intermediate transformer outputs. The central idea is that carrying every intermediate vector through the model can involve unnecessary computation. Progressively eliminating less significant vectors offers a way to reduce inference time while largely preserving predictive accuracy.

The method uses self-attention to measure the significance of word vectors and decide which ones to remove. It also augments the model and its loss function to learn how many vectors should be eliminated. These two decisions address both the identity of the retained information and the amount of computation reduced.

On GLUE, the authors report inference-time reductions of up to 4.5 times relative to BERT with less than 1% accuracy loss, alongside a better accuracy-time tradeoff than prior methods. Applied to ALBERT, the method reaches reductions of up to 6.8 times with less than 1% accuracy loss. These reported maxima show that intermediate-vector reduction can also benefit an already compressed model.
icml-2020-power-bert-accelerating-bert-i.tldr: PoWER-BERT learns to remove intermediate word vectors, reporting up to 4.5-fold faster BERT inference with less than 1% accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Private aggregation must balance accuracy, communication, and assumptions about whom users trust. Central differential privacy offers high accuracy, whereas local differential privacy incurs substantial accuracy costs under weaker trust assumptions. This paper works in the shuffled model, where anonymous messages provide another setting for designing private aggregation algorithms.

The authors develop communication-efficient algorithms for two basic tasks: summing binary values and constructing histograms with a moderate number of buckets. They achieve accuracy arbitrarily close to central differential privacy algorithms. At the same time, the expected communication per user essentially matches the communication needed without privacy constraints.

The combination matters because privacy mechanisms can otherwise impose costs on both the quality of aggregate statistics and the volume of messages users send. Here, the stated accuracy result is paired with a particularly small expected communication burden. Experimental evaluations, including comparisons with Randomized Response and RAPPOR, demonstrate the practicality of the proposed algorithms for these aggregation tasks.
icml-2020-private-counting-from-anonymou.tldr: Shuffled private counting achieves accuracy arbitrarily close to central privacy methods with nearly nonprivate expected communication per user.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can become unstable when function approximation, off-policy data, and Bellman updates are combined. This paper investigates whether the state representation itself can provide stability. It formally establishes that nontrivial representations exist under which the standard SARSA algorithm remains stable even when learning off-policy.

The authors examine representations derived from a policy’s transition matrix, including proto-value functions. They assess them through three connected concerns: approximation error, stability, and how easily they can be estimated. For the general case of a defective transition matrix, a Schur basis provides convergence guarantees, but estimating that basis from samples is difficult.

When the reward function is fixed, an orthogonal basis of the associated Krylov subspace is identified as an even better choice. Experiments then show that stable representations can be learned with stochastic gradient descent. This makes representation learning a theoretically motivated route toward stability and suggests opportunities for deep networks, without claiming a general stability guarantee for arbitrary learned neural representations.
icml-2020-representations-for-stable-off.tldr: Certain state representations guarantee stable off-policy SARSA, and experiments show stable representations can be learned through stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes can be costly to apply to large datasets because their kernel calculations demand substantial memory and computation. Exploiting structure in the kernel matrix can reduce those costs, but mixtures of nonstationary processes are harder for existing structured methods to handle. This paper extends structured kernel interpolation to processes with a nonstationary phase.

The approach uses multiple sets of inducing points that are not equally spaced. These sets account for the nonstationarity while recovering Toeplitz and Kronecker structure in the kernel matrix. Recovering that structure is what enables efficient inference and learning of the kernel within the proposed framework.

The authors focus particularly on separating nonstationary sources, a problem that arises in spatial and temporal biomedical data. Demonstrations include numerical examples and large biomedical problems of this kind. The contribution connects a more flexible treatment of changing source behavior with structured matrix computation, allowing the framework to address mixtures that previous scalable approaches could not easily accommodate.
icml-2020-scalable-gaussian-process-sepa.tldr: Multiple nonuniform inducing-point sets enable structured, scalable Gaussian-process inference for separating sources with nonstationary phase.

paragraphs: Synthetic training examples could help heartbeat classification, but generating useful electrocardiograms requires capturing a dynamic biological system. The different parts of that system interact in complicated ways. This paper draws on mathematical heart simulators to bring existing knowledge of those dynamics into the generation of ECG training data.

The method incorporates a system of ordinary differential equations representing heart dynamics into the optimization of a generative adversarial network. The simulator therefore participates in the generative learning process. Its role is to help create biologically plausible ECG examples that can be used for the downstream classification task.

The authors empirically evaluate the approach and find that incorporating heart-simulation knowledge during generation improves ECG classification. The result connects the usefulness of synthetic examples to the scientific structure included in their creation. More broadly, the work demonstrates a way to combine a physiological process model with learned generation, using performance on heartbeat classification as evidence that the combination produces useful training data.
icml-2020-simgans-simulator-based-genera.tldr: SimGANs incorporate heart-dynamics equations into adversarial generation to create ECG training examples that improve reported classification performance.

paragraphs: Even a one-layer neural network can present a difficult learning problem. This paper establishes superpolynomial lower bounds for learning such networks under Gaussian input distributions. The results concern broad algorithm classes and commonly used activations, including ReLU and sigmoid, showing that shallow architecture alone does not ensure efficient learnability.

For regression with squared loss, the authors prove a polynomial-time barrier to achieving small test error with gradient descent, even when it is run on any classifier. This extends earlier results that required small batches and sufficiently smooth classifiers. For classification, the lower bound covers any statistical query algorithm, giving a broader algorithmic obstruction in that setting.

The proof uses a newly constructed family of simple neural networks that are exactly orthogonal under every spherically symmetric distribution. That construction provides the core of the hardness argument. The conclusions establish difficult learning instances under the stated distribution and algorithmic conditions; they do not say that every one-layer network is difficult to learn in practice.
icml-2020-superpolynomial-lower-bounds-f.tldr: The paper proves superpolynomial learning lower bounds for one-layer networks under Gaussian inputs, covering gradient descent and statistical query methods.

paragraphs: An agent may need to complete a formally specified task before it fully understands what different parts of its environment mean. This paper studies tasks expressed in temporal logic when relevant state properties are only partially known. The agent represents uncertainty about those properties, called atomic propositions, through probabilistic beliefs.

The proposed strategy combines perception and planning so that decisions account for semantic uncertainty. As new sensory measurements arrive, the agent updates its beliefs and adapts its plan accordingly. The planning method also provides probabilistic guarantees on task success, connecting the uncertainty representation to the likelihood of satisfying the assigned task.

The authors evaluate the approach on finite-horizon tasks in planar navigation environments. Their empirical results show reliable task performance and improvement as knowledge of the environment increases. The finding supports planning that explicitly tracks uncertain meaning: additional observations can change both what the agent believes about its surroundings and how it acts to complete the task.
icml-2020-task-oriented-active-perceptio.tldr: The method adapts perception and planning to uncertain environmental properties, providing probabilistic task guarantees and improved navigation performance as knowledge grows.

paragraphs: Simplex-valued observations describe quantities such as proportions whose components sum to one. They occur in applications including transfer learning and neural-network compression. This paper identifies systematic bias and numerical difficulties in standard modeling choices, including the Dirichlet distribution and related losses, particularly when flexible neural networks feed into these models.

The authors introduce the continuous categorical distribution as a new exponential family for this data type. It extends the continuous Bernoulli to the multivariate setting. The proposed distribution yields a well-behaved probabilistic loss with unbiased estimators while retaining mathematical simplicity comparable to the Dirichlet, addressing both statistical and computational concerns raised by the existing choices.

The paper studies theoretical properties and develops sampling methods compatible with the reparameterization trick, then evaluates those methods. Empirical comparisons cover simulations, multi-party election data, and neural-network compression, with the continuous categorical outperforming standard alternatives in these settings. The contribution offers a new probabilistic model whose stated benefits extend from estimation properties to applied learning tasks.
icml-2020-the-continuous-categorical-a-n.tldr: The continuous categorical models simplex-valued data with a tractable probabilistic loss, addressing stated bias and numerical problems in standard alternatives.

paragraphs: Infinite-width limits simplify neural-network training enough to make theoretical analysis more tractable. Two major descriptions are mean-field theory and the constant-kernel, or NTK, limit. This paper introduces a framework linking them and uses it to examine how well such limits represent finite networks.

The framework produces a discrete-time mean-field limit with a convergence theorem. The authors show that this limit gives a more reasonable approximation than NTK when learning rates are not very small. It also suggests another limiting model that is distinct from both mean-field and NTK descriptions, expanding the range of possible theoretical approximations.

The analysis further shows that the optimizer matters: for networks with more than two hidden layers, RMSProp has a nontrivial discrete-time mean-field limit, whereas gradient descent does not. Overall, the results identify considerable limitations in both familiar limits as approximations to finite networks. They motivate more accurate limiting descriptions that account for the training conditions rather than treating infinite width as a single universal approximation.
icml-2020-towards-a-general-theory-of-in.tldr: A unified framework links mean-field and NTK limits while showing how learning rates, depth, and optimizers affect their relevance to finite networks.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification requires useful predictions from very few examples of a task. Meta-learning produces feature extractors that perform strongly in this setting, but the reasons for their success are not well understood. This paper investigates what distinguishes those learned representations from representations produced by conventional training.

The authors introduce and verify several hypotheses about why meta-learned models perform better. They then use that investigation to develop a regularizer that improves ordinary training routines for few-shot classification. The contribution therefore connects an explanatory study of feature representations with a concrete modification to how standard models are trained.

In many cases, the resulting routine outperforms meta-learning while running an order of magnitude faster. The qualification matters: the reported advantage holds in many evaluated cases, rather than being a universal ranking of training methods. The finding suggests that understanding the properties of effective representations can make some benefits of meta-learning accessible through a faster conventional training procedure.
icml-2020-unraveling-meta-learning-under.tldr: Studying meta-learned features yields a regularizer that improves standard few-shot training and often beats meta-learning while running substantially faster.
